name: Olga Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll be honest, I'm a bit practical about all this, so don't expect speeches.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do interior fit-out on a block of eighty flats by the ring road, for a firm that does the inside once the shell is up. Right now I'm on stud walls, the metal and timber frames for the plasterboard, and I'm learning to hang doors. A good day is when the doors close properly first time; a bad day is when the plasterers are waiting on me and the site manager's on the radio every ten minutes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a shared house in a commuter town forty minutes out, because the city's too dear. I've got about three weeks of money saved, and I send a bit to my mum each month because her hours got cut at the bakery. There's only one other fit-out firm round my way, so I hang on to this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, right, so not much changes, back to work. At work there'd be a few jokes about the site manager's new tablet being a waste of money. Online I'd maybe like a post or two, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same pressures. The block finishes in eight months, and the firm only keeps people on if they win the next contract. If they don't, I'm looking at a long commute or agency work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get good at doors, because door hangers get kept on. I'd try to save an extra fifty a month by cooking on Sundays for the week. I use the chatbot sometimes to write a polite message to the site manager, and I'd keep doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A little bit of the old background worry about the end of the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said door hangers get kept on. Why is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's fussy work and a bad door costs the firm a callback. If you can hang a fire door so it closes on its own and seals right, you're worth keeping. I'm maybe half as quick as Tariq, the bloke who's training me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens with your mum if your work stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I stop sending money, and she'd have to ask my brother, and he's got two kids already. I'd hate that more than being out of work myself.

say: I'd say **not much changes**, so back to work.
I'd join the jokes about the site manager's **new tablet** being wasted money.
think: The block finishes in **eight months** and the firm needs the next contract.
Otherwise she faces a **long commute** or agency work.
do: Get good at **hanging doors**, since door hangers get kept on.
Save an extra **fifty a month** by cooking on Sundays.
Keep using the **chatbot** to write polite messages to the site manager.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with the old background worry about the **contract ending**.
S0.quote: If you can hang a fire door so it closes on its own and seals right, you're worth keeping.
fieldNote: She chooses a **fussy skill** as her job security.
Sending money to her **mum** raises her stakes beyond herself.
AI use is **light and practical**: polite messages.
She sounds steady but the **contract end** sits under everything.

steps.text: Practise hanging fire doors until she matches her trainer's speed
Cook for the week on Sundays to save fifty a month
Keep working on the ring road block until it finishes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for office work and leave it there. At work I'd say the firm should use it for the snagging lists, which are a nightmare. Online, nothing much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my hands-on bit is fine for now, but the firm will shrink the office and push us harder with tighter programmes. An app telling the site manager each door should take forty minutes would hurt, because I take an hour and ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the snagging app when the others start using it, and get decent at it, since I'm steady, not first. I'd ask Tariq if I can shadow him two Saturdays a month to speed up. And I'd keep sending money to Mum but maybe a bit less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like being timed at something you're still learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The woman in the site office who does the snagging lists and orders the ironmongery. Her whole job is the thing it does. She's lovely, and she's got a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd cut what you send your mum. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. I'd tell her it's just for a few months while I get faster. She'd say don't worry, and then worry.

say: I'd say AI makes sense for **office work**.
I'd suggest the firm use it for **snagging lists**, which are a nightmare.
think: Her hands-on work is fine, but the firm will push **tighter programmes**.
An app will say each door takes **forty minutes**; she takes seventy.
do: Learn the **snagging app** once others are using it.
Shadow her trainer **two Saturdays** a month to speed up.
Send her mum **a bit less** for a few months.
feel: **Uneasy**, like being **timed** at something she's still learning.
S1.quote: An app telling the site manager each door should take forty minutes would hurt, because I take an hour and ten.
fieldNote: She fears being **measured**, not replaced, in this scenario.
She feels for the **site office worker** whose tasks AI takes.
She adopts tech **once proven**, true to her steady nature.
Cutting help to her **mum** is her hardest trade-off.

steps.text: Learn the snagging app once the crew is using it
Shadow her trainer two Saturdays a month to hang doors faster
Send her mum less money for a few months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd better see what the government does, and quick. At work I'd say the fit-out lads have until 2031, roughly. I wouldn't post much, maybe share a news story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be worried for 2031. Fit-out is repetitive in a block like this, eighty identical flats, same walls, same doors. That's exactly the kind of job a robot would start on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving hard right away, every spare pound, aiming for three months by 2031. I'd look at what jobs need a person in a room with people, maybe kitchen fitting in old houses where nothing's square. I'd use AI more to plan it, find courses, write a CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Not panic, but close to it some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why kitchens in old houses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every old house is different, wonky floors, walls out of plumb, a customer standing over you. A robot in an eighty-flat block is easy; a robot in a Victorian kitchen with a dog and a granny is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in the three years from 2028 before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork side goes, the orders and programmes. We'd get told exactly what to do by a screen, and probably more flats per week. And everyone on site would be quietly looking for the exit.

say: I'd say we need to see what the **government** does, quickly.
I'd tell the fit-out crew we have **until 2031**, roughly.
think: Fit-out in **eighty identical flats** is exactly where robots start.
She'd be truly **worried for 2031**, when robots reach hands-on site work.
do: Save every spare pound, aiming for **three months** by 2031.
Move toward **kitchen fitting** in old, uneven houses.
Use **AI more** to find courses and write a CV.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, close to panic some nights.
S2.quote: A robot in an eighty-flat block is easy; a robot in a Victorian kitchen with a dog and a granny is not.
fieldNote: She reads **repetition** as the danger in her current block.
Her escape route is **messy old houses** with customers present.
She expects **2028–2031** to mean screens directing work and more flats per week.
She'd step up AI use as a **planning tool** for herself.

steps.text: Save every spare pound toward three months of costs by 2031
Move into kitchen fitting in old houses
Use AI to find courses and rewrite her CV

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning. At work I'd say the smart ones will learn kitchens and bathrooms now. Online, nothing different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel I have time to get a proper trade certificate. Eight years till robots means I could be a qualified kitchen fitter, maybe with my own van. But I'd still be in a room in a shared house, saving pennies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd sign up for a kitchen fitting course at the college, two evenings a week. I'd keep the fit-out job meanwhile and save. And I'd ask Tariq if he knows anyone fitting kitchens who'd take me on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with the usual worry about money in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't panic-save. I'd spend a bit on tools, a good mitre saw, because you need your own kit for kitchens. With two years I'd keep every penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you feel the plan had worked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting called back by a customer because they liked my work. That's never happened to me. In a block of eighty flats, nobody even knows who hung the door.

say: I'd call **five years** fair warning for anyone on a building site.
I'd tell the crew to **learn kitchens** and bathrooms now.
think: **Eight years** to robots is enough to become a qualified kitchen fitter.
She'd still be renting a **room** and saving pennies.
do: Sign up for a **kitchen fitting course**, two evenings a week.
Buy a good **mitre saw** for her own kit.
Ask her trainer about **weekend work** with a kitchen fitter.
feel: **Hopeful**, with the usual **money worry** behind it.
S3.quote: In a block of eighty flats, nobody even knows who hung the door.
fieldNote: More time lets her **invest in tools** instead of hoarding cash.
She wants **recognition** from customers, which site work never gives.
Her plan is clear but rests on **thin savings**.
The fit-out job still faces **robots by 2034**, which keeps her anxious.

steps.text: Take the college kitchen fitting course two evenings a week
Buy a good mitre saw and start her own tool kit
Fit kitchens on weekends with someone her trainer knows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, fine, plenty of time to plan. At work I'd say the same. I don't think I'd post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years till robots on site, I'd be forty. That's enough to have my own small business fitting kitchens. I'd feel all right about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the kitchen course over two years rather than rushing it. I'd keep the job on the flats and save a bit, then start a few weekend jobs. I'd wait to see which AI tools the good fitters actually use before buying anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Uneasy round the edges, because the contract still ends in eight months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the real worry is still the contract, not the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, honestly. Robots in thirteen years is a story. The flats finishing in eight months is real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to worry, I've got a plan, and for once I'd mean it. She'd still worry. That's mums.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty of time to plan.
I'd say the same at work and **not post** about it.
think: **Thirteen years** to robots lets her build a small kitchen business by forty.
She'd **feel all right** about that timeline.
do: Take the **kitchen course** over two years.
Start **weekend jobs** once she has some savings.
**Wait to see** which AI tools good fitters use.
feel: **Steady**, uneasy round the edges about the **contract ending**.
S4.quote: Robots in thirteen years is a story. The flats finishing in eight months is real life.
fieldNote: With a decade, her worry returns to the **ordinary contract end**.
She'd pace her training **slowly** rather than rushing.
She waits for **proof** before adopting tools, as usual.
She'd reassure her **mum** and mean it this time.

steps.text: Take the kitchen fitting course over two years
Fit kitchens on weekends once savings allow
Watch which AI tools good kitchen fitters use first

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Eighty identical flats is what robots learn on, and I'd only have three years. What would help is a cheap evening course in kitchen fitting and some help with tools, because the kit costs more than I save in a year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family. Lots of us on site send money home, and if we lose work it's not just us who goes short.

headlineQuote: Lots of us on site send money home, and if we lose work it's not just us who goes short.
portrait: Olga is **27**, a junior **fit-out** carpenter on an eighty-flat block, renting a room.
She sends money to her **mum** and has about three weeks saved.
She's **practical**, uses AI lightly and adopts tools once others prove them.
She sees **repetitive block work** as robot territory and aims for kitchens in old houses.
Her day-to-day worry stays the **contract ending** in eight months.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her repetitive block work is what robots learn first.
whatWouldHelp: A cheap **evening course** in kitchen fitting and help buying **tools**.
